kp.k: Underwriting document review shows reported productivity gains
kp.d: In this Harvey company-blog interview published May 8, 2026, Bryan Dressler reports a 300% productivity increase, largely from comparing manual due diligence report review with standardised prompting. He gives a task-time comparison of an hour and a half to two hours versus about 15 minutes. The introduction dates his team's adoption to early 2025. These are customer-reported results in M&A warranty and indemnity underwriting, rather than findings about practicing lawyers generally.
qs: Since adopting Harvey in early 2025, his team has seen a 300% increase in productivity.
The number I typically cite is a 300% increase in productivity.
What used to take an hour and a half to two hours can now be done in about 15 minutes.

kp.k: Time savings enable deeper diligence analysis
kp.d: Dressler describes augmentation beyond faster report review: Harvey creates time to compare data-room material with what diligence reports reflect. He characterises this expanded analytical scope as checking the diligence itself, rather than merely completing the existing task more quickly.
qs: Without a tool like Harvey, I’d only have time to review the reports themselves.
There wouldn’t be enough time to connect the dots between what’s in the data room and what’s reflected in the diligence.
So it’s not just about efficiency, it creates the opportunity to do a deeper level of analysis.
It’s effectively due diligence on the due diligence.

kp.k: Productivity follows a learning and verification J-curve
kp.d: Dressler cautions that gains are not immediate: initial experimentation, output validation and trust-building require effort before users can reliably structure requests and obtain usable results quickly. He defines power users by their instinct to consider AI before defaulting to manual methods, even when that initially takes more work.
qs: A power user is someone who, when faced with a problem, instinctively asks: “How can I use an AI tool to solve this?” rather than defaulting to a manual or traditional approach, even if that takes more effort upfront.
When you first start using Harvey or similar tools, you don’t see immediate productivity gains.
It follows more of a J-curve — you’re experimenting, validating outputs, and building trust.
But once you reach that point of confidence, the process becomes much more efficient — you know how to structure the request and get to a usable result quickly.

kp.k: Growth expectations motivate managed AI adoption
kp.d: Dressler links adoption within his team of eight to an expectation of 25% year-over-year growth and limited working hours, presenting better tools as an alternative to compromising quality. He reports uneven uptake and describes usage tracking as a directional management tool for setting expectations and encouraging engagement; some initially hesitant colleagues become highly active users.
qs: I manage a team of eight.
If we’re expected to grow 25% year over year, there are only so many hours available.
You either compromise on quality, or you find better ways of working — and for us, that means adopting tools like Harvey.
I use usage tracking as a directional tool, setting expectations and encouraging people to engage.
And in many cases, the people who were initially hesitant end up becoming some of the most active users.

kp.k: Effective AI use is a learnable communication skill
kp.d: Dressler leans toward power users being made rather than born. While technological comfort helps, he argues that learning to communicate with the tool lowers the barrier to effective use. Motivations include staying ahead, efficiency and maintaining balance, rather than technical expertise alone.
qs: I lean toward them being made.
It helps if you’re already comfortable with new technology, but this is different — you can become highly effective just by learning how to communicate with the tool.
For some, it’s about staying ahead of the curve. For others, it’s about working more efficiently and maintaining balance.
You don’t need to be technical to get value, you just need to be willing to engage.

kp.k: Prompt templates and task decomposition underpin workflow improvement
kp.d: Dressler recommends developing prompt engineering through structured inputs, defined outputs and consistent templates, then breaking complex tasks into smaller steps and chaining prompts into workflows. His practical standard is incremental improvement over work performed without Harvey, rather than perfect tool use.
qs: The core skill you’re developing is prompt engineering, understanding how to structure inputs, define outputs, and use consistent templates.
Then there’s a second layer: breaking complex tasks into smaller steps and chaining those prompts into a workflow.
My framework is simple: the benchmark isn’t perfect use of Harvey, it’s what your work would look like without it.
If you’re improving on that baseline, you’re making progress.

kp.k: Manual diligence review is predicted to recede
kp.d: Dressler predicts that the work will no longer centre on groups manually reviewing due diligence reports in five years, while explicitly acknowledging uncertainty about its future form. This is his forward-looking expectation, not a demonstrated staffing or employment outcome.
qs: I don’t know exactly what this work will look like in five years, but I’m confident it won’t be a group of people sitting in a room manually reviewing due diligence reports.

pts.k: Dressler claims that Harvey increases productivity and enables deeper analysis in M&A warranty and indemnity underwriting, and predicts that manual due diligence review will no longer define this work in five years.
pts.d: Bryan Dressler, Markel’s Director of Warranty & Indemnity, reports a 300% productivity increase, citing a reduction in due diligence report review time from 90–120 minutes to about 15 minutes. He says the time saved allows comparison of data-room material with diligence findings, rather than merely reviewing reports. He describes adoption as an initially costly learning process followed by efficiency gains. He also argues that effective use is learnable without technical expertise, through structuring prompts, specifying outputs, using templates and breaking complex tasks into linked steps. His five-year prediction concerns the disappearance of predominantly manual review workflows, not an explicit forecast of job losses.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Dressler’s account of his own team’s experience and a task-level time comparison, presented in a Harvey company-blog interview.
pts.d: Dressler grounds the productivity claim in comparing manual report review with running a standardised prompt across due diligence reports. The article supplies the reported percentage and task durations but does not explain their calculation or aggregation, provide a sample size, or present an independent evaluation. Claims about deeper analysis, learning and adoption draw on his managerial and practical experience. Usage tracking is described as a directional adoption tool, not a measure establishing output quality. The five-year forecast is a statement of confidence rather than a separately evidenced projection.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Reported gains follow adoption in early 2025; Dressler conditions efficiency on learning and validating outputs, with a separate five-year workflow prediction.
pts.d: The Harvey Team’s introduction dates adoption to early 2025, and the interview was published May 8, 2026. Dressler says gains are not immediate: users first experiment, check outputs and build confidence before efficiently obtaining usable results. He identifies communication with the tool, consistent templates and decomposition of complex tasks as enabling skills. Adoption varies across the team and, in his account, follows visible impact. His growth rationale is conditional on an expectation of 25% year-over-year growth. His prediction looks five years ahead, approximately to 2031 relative to publication, while expressly acknowledging uncertainty about the precise future workflow.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct subjects are Dressler and his eight-person underwriting team at Markel, rather than practising lawyers or the legal-services market generally.
pts.d: This is a legal-document-intensive insurance underwriting example: the team assesses whether M&A due diligence supports warranties in share purchase agreements. Dressler describes faster review, greater scope for cross-document analysis and a way to address growth pressures without compromising quality. Team members are expected to engage with AI, and their skill development shifts toward prompting and workflow design. He also identifies efficiency and work–life balance as motivations for users. The source does not establish effects on law-firm staffing, legal fees or access to justice.
